title: Chapter 9.5 — Solving Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine having a master key that unlocks any quadratic equation. By completing the square on the general equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, we get the Quadratic Formula — a single formula that solves every quadratic, no matter how messy the coefficients!

formulaCard.title: Quadratic Formula
notes: $a, b, c$ are from $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, $a \ne 0$.
If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, there are no real solutions.
If $b^2 - 4ac = 0$, there is exactly one real solution (repeated).

explanation: The [[kw:Quadratic Formula]] gives the solutions of any quadratic equation in standard form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$:
$$ x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} $$
The formula comes from completing the square on the general quadratic equation.
To use it, identify $a$, $b$, and $c$ from the standard form, substitute, and simplify.
The expression under the radical, $b^2 - 4ac$, is called the [[kw:discriminant]]. It tells how many real solutions exist.

confusionCorner.body: If $b$ is negative, $-b$ becomes positive. In Example A, $b = -5$, so $-b = 5$. Also, $b^2$ is always positive, so $(-5)^2 = 25$. [[imp:Be careful with signs when substituting.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch the Signs in $b$!

explanation: Real-world data can be modeled by quadratic functions. To find when a certain value occurs, set the function equal to that value and solve the resulting quadratic equation.
Example: Wolf breeding pairs $y = 0.20x^2 + 1.8x - 3$, where $x$ is years since 1990. Find when $y = 35$.
Use the Quadratic Formula: $a = 0.20, b = 1.8, c = -38$.
Solutions: $x = 10$ (year 2000) and $x = -19$ (reject, since $x$ must be $\ge 0$).

formulaCard.title: Discriminant

explanation: The [[kw:discriminant]] of a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ is $D = b^2 - 4ac$.
If $D > 0$, the equation has [[imp:two real solutions]] (two x-intercepts).
If $D = 0$, the equation has [[imp:one real solution]] (one x-intercept; the vertex touches the x-axis).
If $D < 0$, the equation has [[imp:no real solutions]] (no x-intercepts).
You can use the discriminant to quickly check the number of real solutions without solving the equation.

visuals.title: Discriminant and Number of Real Solutions

confusionCorner.body: Always put the equation in standard form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ before computing the discriminant. If you use the wrong sign for $c$, the discriminant will be wrong.
confusionCorner.title: Standard Form First!

discoveryHook.scenario: You don't always need the full Quadratic Formula to know how many solutions an equation has. The discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ is a quick detective — it tells you if there are two, one, or zero real solutions, just by checking a simple calculation!

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{1. Factoring} \quad \text{2. Graphing} \quad \text{3. Square Roots} \quad \text{4. Completing the Square} \quad \text{5. Quadratic Formula} $$
formulaCard.title: Five Methods for Solving Quadratic Equations

explanation: Different quadratic equations are best solved by different methods.
**Factoring:** Best when the quadratic easily factors into integers. Quick and exact.
**Graphing:** Good for visualizing solutions and approximating. Use technology for precision.
**Square Roots:** Fastest for equations of the form $ax^2 + c = 0$ or $(x-h)^2 = d$.
**Completing the Square:** Efficient when $a=1$ and $b$ is even. Also useful for finding vertex form.
**Quadratic Formula:** Works for any quadratic. Use when other methods are difficult or messy. Always gives exact solutions.

discoveryHook.scenario: You now have five tools to solve quadratics. Choosing the right tool makes the job faster and easier. Factoring for nice integers, square roots for $x^2 = d$, completing the square when $a=1$ and $b$ is even, and the Quadratic Formula as the universal backup.

confusionCorner.body: If you can't find factors quickly, switch to the Quadratic Formula. It's designed for exactly that situation. [[imp:Don't waste time trying to factor an unfactorable quadratic.]]
confusionCorner.title: Don't Force Factoring

discoveryHook.scenario: The Quadratic Formula is your reliable friend for any quadratic. Follow this blueprint — standard form, identify, discriminant, formula, interpret — and you'll solve any quadratic equation with confidence, whether in pure math or real‑world modeling!

teacherCues: Post the blueprint: 1) Write in standard form. 2) Identify a, b, c. 3) Compute discriminant. 4) Plug into formula and simplify. 5) Interpret solutions.
Emphasize that the discriminant step can be done first to know how many solutions to expect.
blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Mastering the Quadratic Formula

confusionCorner.title: Negative Discriminant? Stop.
confusionCorner.body: If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, the equation has no real solutions. Don't try to take the square root of a negative number in this course. The answer is simply 'no real solutions'.

explanation: Understand: Ensure the equation is in standard form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$.
Solve – Identify: Note $a$, $b$, $c$ (including their signs).
Solve – Discriminant: Compute $D = b^2 - 4ac$. This tells you the number of real solutions (2 if $D>0$, 1 if $D=0$, 0 if $D<0$).
Solve – Formula: Substitute into $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}$. Simplify the radical if possible. If $D$ is a perfect square, solutions are rational.
Conclude: State the exact solutions and/or decimal approximations. In word problems, reject solutions that don't fit the context.
